newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope near tears recalls professors' wartime arrest.
newsitem.headline: Pope near tears recalls professors' wartime arrest.

text.p: Pope John Paul was moved close to tears on Sunday when he visited his Alma Mater and recalled the day in 1939 when Nazi occupying forces deported nearly 150 professors to concentration camps.

"I was talking to some of them that day. They never went home, they never came back," the Pope said in unprepared remarks at the end of a speech to contemporary professors gathered in the Church of Krakow's Jagiellonian university.
"There are many other memories deep in my heart," he said.
A few minutes later, attending a concert in his honour in the university courtyard, the Pope was seen to touch his eye several times while listening to haunting violin music.

On November 6, 1939, a month after Nazi German forces invaded the Pope's native land, their Gestapo security police rounded up 144 professors and assistant professors, as well as some students, and sent them to concentration camps.

The university, founded in 1364, was shut and vandalised or robbed of its equipment as part of a policy to destroy Polish intellectual life, but students continued to learn underground, including the young Karol Wojtyla.

The visit to his university, where he once taught, was the culmination of an emotional day that began when he celebrated a three-hour-long mass before a crowd police estimated at more than 1.5 million people.
His spokesman said the 77-year-old Roman Catholic leader was holding up very well and may visit Poland again.
"I refuse to accept the notion that this is the Pope's last trip to Poland," chief Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls told a news conference.
Bishop Tadeusz Pieronek, secretary of the Polish bishops' conference, also said there was reason to believe the Pope would visit Poland as several invitations had been made for him to come next year.
Navarro-Valls said the trip through areas of his youth was an "extraordinary" experience for the Pope.
"He is living through a lot of memories," he said, adding that the Pope was full of "intellectual curiosity" about where his country was heading.
"The Pope has held up perfectly well," Navarro-Valls said, sleeping well, though rising early as usual.
"There are no signs of any particular problems," he said.

"I'm not saying that the Pope in 1997 is the same as he was in 1978 when he was elected, but he shows he has the capacity to do the work," Navarro-Valls added, suggesting that 11 days on the road home in Poland were perhaps less fatiguing than 16-hour days mostly spent behind a desk at the Vatican.
Sunday's crowd was the biggest of the trip so far. A sea of people turned out at the Blonia meadows in Krakow, where John Paul lived for more than 20 years as priest, bishop and cardinal.
Speaking in a strong voice, the Pontiff told the pilgrims that, now they had regained freedom after nearly half a century of communism, they should use it to spread love and truth.
Wearing resplendent gold robes billowing in a soft breeze, he told the crowd that 10 years ago "we had before us the problem of the discovery of freedom".

In 1987, the country was still run by communists. Two years later in 1989 they gave way to Eastern Europe's first democratically-elected government, headed by the Solidarity trade union, which the Pope unflaggingly backed.
To the Pope's joy after years of praying for a more united Europe, the domino-like fall of the Soviet bloc was under way.
"Now divine providence is putting a new task before us: to love and serve. To love in deed and in truth," he said.
At the mass the Pope canonised Queen Jadwiga, who died in 1399 at the age of 25 after helping to spread Christianity to neighbouring countries, particularly Lithuania.
